items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "population density".
items.answer: The number of people per unit area, usually people per km²; total population ÷ land area
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the number of people per unit area, usually people per km²; total population ÷ land area. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: "Population distribution today is mainly the result of climate." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Climate matters, but human factors (economic development, history, politics, accessibility) now strongly influence distribution, e.g. the growth of Dubai in a desert.
items.markingKey: Climate matters, but human factors (economic development, history, politics, accessibility) now strongly influence distribution, e.g. the growth of Dubai in a desert. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how human factors can produce high population densities in physically unfavourable areas.
items.answer: Economic opportunity (e.g. oil wealth in Gulf cities), political decisions (planned capitals such as Brasília), technology (desalination, air-conditioning) and historical trade routes can attract and support large populations despite harsh climate.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Economic opportunity (e.g. oil wealth in Gulf cities), political decisions (planned capitals such as Brasília), technology (desalination, air-conditioning) and historical trade routes can attract and support large populations despite harsh climate. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: On a map at a scale of 1:25,000, the straight-line distance between two sampling sites on a beach transect measures 1.8 cm. Calculate the real distance in kilometres.
items.markingKey: M1 multiply by the scale; A1 0.45 km (unit conversion correct).

items.stem: The Netherlands has a population of about 17.9 million and an area of 41,850 km²; Canada has about 40.1 million people in 9,984,670 km². (a) Calculate the population density of each. (b) How many times more densely populated is the denser country? (c) Explain why national density can hide uneven distribution, using one of these countries.
items.answer: (a) the Netherlands: 427.7 /km²; Canada: 4.0 /km² (b) ≈ 106.5 times (c) e.g. most people cluster in favourable areas (coasts, river valleys, cities) while deserts/mountains are almost empty.
items.markingKey: (a) A1 427.7, A1 4.0. (b) A1 106.5. (c) R1 uneven distribution explained with a physical or human factor.

items.stem: Examine the relative importance of physical and human factors in explaining the population distribution of one named country.
items.answer: Indicative content: Award for specific locations, figures and factors: e.g. Brazil - coastal concentration (São Paulo, Rio) from colonial history and the coastal economy; sparse Amazon interior (dense forest, poor soils, disease) but growth along BR-highways and in Manaus Free Trade Zone; planned capital Brasília 1960; judgement balancing both.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Award for specific locations, figures and factors: e.g. Brazil - coastal concentration (São Paulo, Rio) from colonial history and the coastal economy; sparse Amazon interior (dense forest, poor soils, disease) but growth along BR-highways and in Manaus Free Trade Zone; planned capital Brasília 1960; judgement balancing both. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The number of people per unit area, usually people per km²; total population ÷ land area"?
items.answer: population density
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of population density.

items.stem: Distinguish between population density and population distribution.
items.answer: Density is a numerical measure (people per km²) for an area; distribution describes the spatial pattern of where people are located (clustered, linear, dispersed) and is shown on a dot map.
items.markingKey: Density is a numerical measure (people per km²) for an area; distribution describes the spatial pattern of where people are located (clustered, linear, dispersed) and is shown on a dot map. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why population density is a limited measure of population distribution.
items.answer: Density is an average for a whole area; it hides uneven clustering within it (e.g. Australia averages 3.5 /km² but about 85% of people live within 50 km of the coast), and ignores land quality, so physiological density may be more meaningful.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Density is an average for a whole area; it hides uneven clustering within it (e.g. Australia averages 3.5 /km² but about 85% of people live within 50 km of the coast), and ignores land quality, so physiological density may be more meaningful. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Suggest why Java holds over half of Indonesia's population on about 7% of its land area.
items.answer: Fertile volcanic soils support intensive wet-rice farming; colonial and post-colonial investment and the capital Jakarta concentrated jobs and infrastructure on Java.
items.markingKey: Fertile volcanic soils support intensive wet-rice farming; colonial and post-colonial investment and the capital Jakarta concentrated jobs and infrastructure on Java.

items.stem: Briefly describe Japan's Tokaido corridor and explain what it reveals about the role of relief in population distribution.
items.answer: The Tokyo-Nagoya-Osaka belt holds around half of Japan's population on coastal plains, as about 70% of Japan is mountainous. Mountains confine dense settlement to narrow lowland plains.
items.markingKey: Context (The Tokyo-Nagoya-Osaka belt holds around half of Japan's population on coastal plains, as about 70% of Japan is mountainous.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Mountains confine dense settlement to narrow lowland plains. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the role of relief in population distribution.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that physical factors are more important than human factors in explaining global population distribution?
items.answer: Physical factors set broad global limits, but human factors increasingly explain where people cluster within habitable areas.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: large empty areas coincide with deserts, ice caps and high mountains; early agricultural civilisations clustered in fertile river valleys (Nile, Indus, Huang He). Against / limitations: economic opportunity and technology now override physical limits (Gulf cities, Singapore); political and historical factors (colonial ports, planned capitals, migration policies) shape distribution. A supported conclusion might be: Physical factors set broad global limits, but human factors increasingly explain where people cluster within habitable areas. items.stem: State what is meant by the term "megacity".
items.answer: An urban agglomeration with a population of more than 10 million
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an urban agglomeration with a population of more than 10 million. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain how cumulative causation can widen the gap between core and periphery.
items.answer: Initial advantages attract firms and migrants; the multiplier effect creates jobs, tax revenue and services, attracting further investment, while backwash drains young, skilled people and capital from the periphery.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Initial advantages attract firms and migrants; the multiplier effect creates jobs, tax revenue and services, attracting further investment, while backwash drains young, skilled people and capital from the periphery. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Megacities grow only because of rural-urban migration." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Natural increase within the city is often as important as migration, especially where migrants are young adults with high fertility (e.g. Lagos).
items.markingKey: Natural increase within the city is often as important as migration, especially where migrants are young adults with high fertility (e.g. Lagos). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The five largest cities in a census of Kenya (rounded, illustrative): rank 1: 3.5 million; rank 2: 1.25 million; rank 3: 0.99 million; rank 4: 0.61 million; rank 5: 0.58 million. Calculate the primacy index (P1/P2) and the populations predicted by the rank-size rule (Pn = P1/n) for ranks 2-5.
items.answer: primacy = 3.5 / 1.25 = 2.80; predicted 1.75, 1.17, 0.88, 0.70 million
items.markingKey: A1 primacy 2.80; M1 P1/n; A1 predictions;

items.stem: Outline one way in which Lagos, Nigeria shows megacity growth in a low-income country.
items.answer: The city grew from under 1 million in 1960 to around 15 million today, through high natural increase and migration from across Nigeria and West Africa. Growth outpaced infrastructure, creating informal settlements, congestion and an expanding informal economy.
items.markingKey: Context (The city grew from under 1 million in 1960 to around 15 million today, through high natural increase and migration from across Nigeria and West Africa.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Growth outpaced infrastructure, creating informal settlements, congestion and an expanding informal economy. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to megacity growth in a low-income country.

items.stem: Pakistan has 56.3 million urban residents out of 169.7 million. The urban population is growing at 3.2% per year. Calculate (a) the current level of urbanisation, (b) the doubling time of the urban population and (c) the urban population in 10 years if the rate is constant.
items.answer: (a) 33.2% (b) 21.9 years (c) 77.1 million
items.markingKey: A1 33.2%; M1 A1 70/3.2 = 21.9; M1 compound growth A1 77.1 million.

items.stem: Examine the relationship between economic development and population change at the national scale.
items.answer: Indicative content: As development rises, death rates then birth rates fall (DTM); urbanisation and female education reduce fertility; core regions gain migrants; examples Japan, Brazil, Niger; recognise exceptions (Gulf states, China's policy-driven change).
items.markingKey: Indicative content: As development rises, death rates then birth rates fall (DTM); urbanisation and female education reduce fertility; core regions gain migrants; examples Japan, Brazil, Niger; recognise exceptions (Gulf states, China's policy-driven change). items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The flow of people, capital and resources from the periphery to the core that increases regional inequality"?
items.answer: backwash effect
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of backwash effect.

items.stem: Explain why primate cities develop in some countries.
items.answer: Colonial administration and ports concentrated investment in one city; governments locate ministries, airports and universities there; economies of scale attract TNCs, so the city becomes many times larger than the second city (e.g. Lima, Bangkok).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Colonial administration and ports concentrated investment in one city; governments locate ministries, airports and universities there; economies of scale attract TNCs, so the city becomes many times larger than the second city (e.g. Lima, Bangkok). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between spread effects and backwash effects.
items.answer: Backwash effects move resources and people towards the core and increase inequality; spread effects transmit growth outward to the periphery and reduce it.
items.markingKey: Backwash effects move resources and people towards the core and increase inequality; spread effects transmit growth outward to the periphery and reduce it. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using a named country, describe its core-periphery pattern and one consequence for population change.
items.answer: e.g. China: the eastern coastal core (Pearl River Delta, Yangtze River Delta) attracted FDI and hundreds of millions of internal migrants, so interior provinces such as Sichuan and Guizhou lost working-age people and aged faster.
items.markingKey: e.g. China: the eastern coastal core (Pearl River Delta, Yangtze River Delta) attracted FDI and hundreds of millions of internal migrants, so interior provinces such as Sichuan and Guizhou lost working-age people and aged faster.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that the growth of megacities brings more benefits than problems.
items.answer: Benefits are real but depend on governance and investment in infrastructure; without them problems can outweigh benefits for the urban poor.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: economies of scale and agglomeration raise productivity (megacities generate a large share of national GDP); better access to jobs, education and health care than rural areas. Against / limitations: informal settlements, congestion and pollution (Dhaka, Lagos); regional inequality and backwash from the periphery. A supported conclusion might be: Benefits are real but depend on governance and investment in infrastructure; without them problems can outweigh benefits for the urban poor. items.stem: "Government policy can successfully reduce core-periphery inequality." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Policy can narrow but rarely eliminate inequality; success depends on long-term investment and the strength of agglomeration forces.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: China's Western Development Strategy and infrastructure (rail, roads) spread investment inland; the EU Cohesion Fund has supported growth in peripheral regions such as Poland. Arguments challenging it: decades of Cassa per il Mezzogiorno spending did not close Italy's north-south gap; market forces and agglomeration continue to favour the core. Evaluation should weigh places, scales, perspectives and time. items.stem: What is China's hukou?
options: A household registration system that ties access to public services to a person's registered place of origin
items.answer: A household registration system that ties access to public services to a person's registered place of origin
items.markingKey: C. Hukou restrictions are an intervening obstacle and limit migrants' access to urban schools and healthcare.

items.stem: A student claims: "Rural-urban migrants always become better off." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Many migrants end up in informal settlements and insecure informal work; outcomes depend on skills, networks and policy (e.g. hukou restrictions in China).
items.markingKey: Many migrants end up in informal settlements and insecure informal work; outcomes depend on skills, networks and policy (e.g. hukou restrictions in China). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between voluntary migration and forced migration.
items.answer: Voluntary migration is chosen, usually for economic or social reasons; forced migration results from conflict, persecution or disaster, leaving people little or no choice.
items.markingKey: Voluntary migration is chosen, usually for economic or social reasons; forced migration results from conflict, persecution or disaster, leaving people little or no choice. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to Dhaka, Bangladesh, explain how it illustrates environmental push factors in internal migration.
items.answer: The city receives an estimated 1,700 or more migrants a day, many displaced by river-bank erosion and cyclones. Environmental hazards in rural deltas add to economic push factors and accelerate urban growth.
items.markingKey: Context (The city receives an estimated 1,700 or more migrants a day, many displaced by river-bank erosion and cyclones.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Environmental hazards in rural deltas add to economic push factors and accelerate urban growth. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to environmental push factors in internal migration.

items.stem: Canada (population 40 million) has a natural increase of 0.6 per 1,000. In one year it received 334 thousand immigrants and 92 thousand people emigrated. Calculate the net migration rate and the overall rate of population change per 1,000, and state which component dominates.
items.answer: net migration +6.0 per 1,000; total change +6.6 per 1,000; dominant component: migration
items.markingKey: A1 +6.0; M1 natural change + net migration; A1 +6.6; R1 migration.

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Population pyramids described: Village A in rural Sichuan has narrow bars for ages 20-44 and wide bars for 0-14 and 60+; District B in Shenzhen has very wide bars for ages 20-34, especially males, and narrow bars for 60+.

(a) Describe the differences between the two pyramids. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, explain how internal migration accounts for the differences. [6]
items.answer: (a) Village A has a deficit of working-age adults and many children and elderly; District B is dominated by young working adults with few elderly or children. (b) Young adults migrate from rural Sichuan to Shenzhen for factory work, leaving children with grandparents; hukou rules discourage family migration, so destination is adult-dominated.
items.markingKey: (a) Village A has a deficit of working-age adults and many children and elderly; District B is dominated by young working adults with few elderly or children. (b) Young adults migrate from rural Sichuan to Shenzhen for factory work, leaving children with grandparents; hukou rules discourage family migration, so destination is adult-dominated. Credit relevant own knowledge and named examples in (b). items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "push factor".
items.answer: A negative feature of the place of origin that encourages people to leave, e.g. drought, landlessness, lack of services
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a negative feature of the place of origin that encourages people to leave, e.g. drought, landlessness, lack of services. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain how remittances from internal migrants can benefit rural areas.
items.answer: Money sent home funds food, school fees, housing and farm investment; it can reduce poverty and create a multiplier effect, although it can increase dependency on urban income.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Money sent home funds food, school fees, housing and farm investment; it can reduce poverty and create a multiplier effect, although it can increase dependency on urban income. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between pull factors and push factors.
items.answer: Push factors are negative conditions at the origin that drive people away; pull factors are attractions of the destination that draw them; most decisions combine both.
items.markingKey: Push factors are negative conditions at the origin that drive people away; pull factors are attractions of the destination that draw them; most decisions combine both. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: The number of international migrants living in a suburb of Toronto was 85,940 people in 2010 and 100,010 people in 2022. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (100,010 − 85,940) ÷ 85,940 × 100; A1 +16.4% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: Suggest two reasons why migrants from Bihar move to Mumbai and Delhi.
items.answer: Push: low farm incomes, landlessness and floods in Bihar; pull: construction, manufacturing and service jobs with higher wages, and existing migrant networks.
items.markingKey: Push: low farm incomes, landlessness and floods in Bihar; pull: construction, manufacturing and service jobs with higher wages, and existing migrant networks.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that government restrictions are the main factor controlling internal migration flows? Refer to places and scales you have studied.
items.answer: Economic forces drive most internal migration; policy modifies its form more than its overall direction.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: China's hukou has shaped the scale and circular nature of migration; some countries use permits or resettlement programmes. Arguments challenging it: economic differences in wages are the key driver everywhere; environmental hazards and social networks also shape flows. Evaluation should weigh places, scales, perspectives and time. Judgement: Economic forces drive most internal migration; policy modifies its form more than its overall direction. items.stem: According to the UN (2018 revision), how many megacities were there in 2018?
items.markingKey: D. There were 33 megacities in 2018, projected to rise to 43 by 2030, most in Asia and Africa.

items.stem: Approximately what share of the world's population lives in Asia?
items.answer: About 59%
items.markingKey: C. Asia has about 4.8 of the world's 8.1 billion people (≈59%).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "intervening obstacle"?
options: The number of people per unit area, usually people per km²; total population ÷ land area
In Lee's model, a barrier between origin and destination, such as distance, cost, or legal restrictions like China's hukou
The movement of people from the countryside to towns and cities, usually for work, services and higher incomes
The number of people per unit of arable (cultivable) land, a better indicator of pressure on farmland than crude density
items.answer: In Lee's model, a barrier between origin and destination, such as distance, cost, or legal restrictions like China's hukou
items.markingKey: B. "intervening obstacle" is in Lee's model, a barrier between origin and destination, such as distance, cost, or legal restrictions like China's hukou.

items.stem: "Most megacities are in high-income countries." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Only a minority are (e.g. Tokyo, Osaka, New York, Los Angeles, Paris); most are in Asia, Latin America and Africa.
items.markingKey: Only a minority are (e.g. Tokyo, Osaka, New York, Los Angeles, Paris); most are in Asia, Latin America and Africa. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Sana writes: "Population distribution today is mainly the result of climate." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Climate matters, but human factors (economic development, history, politics, accessibility) now strongly influence distribution, e.g. the growth of Dubai in a desert.
items.markingKey: Climate matters, but human factors (economic development, history, politics, accessibility) now strongly influence distribution, e.g. the growth of Dubai in a desert. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Zara writes: "Rural-urban migrants always become better off." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Many migrants end up in informal settlements and insecure informal work; outcomes depend on skills, networks and policy (e.g. hukou restrictions in China).
items.markingKey: Many migrants end up in informal settlements and insecure informal work; outcomes depend on skills, networks and policy (e.g. hukou restrictions in China). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the periphery and the core.
items.answer: The core is the dominant region with high investment, wages and population growth (e.g. coastal eastern China); the periphery is less developed, dependent and often losing population (e.g. western interior China).
items.markingKey: The core is the dominant region with high investment, wages and population growth (e.g. coastal eastern China); the periphery is less developed, dependent and often losing population (e.g. western interior China). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between crude population density and physiological density.
items.answer: Crude density divides population by total land area; physiological density divides by arable land only, so Egypt's physiological density is many times higher than its crude density.
items.markingKey: Crude density divides population by total land area; physiological density divides by arable land only, so Egypt's physiological density is many times higher than its crude density. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why rural-urban migration continues even when urban unemployment is high.
items.answer: Migrants respond to expected rather than actual income (Todaro model); the informal sector offers survival work; social networks reduce risk and costs; rural push factors remain strong.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Migrants respond to expected rather than actual income (Todaro model); the informal sector offers survival work; social networks reduce risk and costs; rural push factors remain strong. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Suggest two challenges faced by a rapidly growing megacity such as Lagos.
items.answer: Housing shortages and informal settlements (e.g. Makoko), traffic congestion and inadequate transport, unreliable electricity and water, flooding of low-lying areas.
items.markingKey: Housing shortages and informal settlements (e.g. Makoko), traffic congestion and inadequate transport, unreliable electricity and water, flooding of low-lying areas.

items.stem: A data table shows the number of births registered in a prefecture of Japan: 1990 - 13,053 births; 2002 - 19,805 births. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (19,805 − 13,053) ÷ 13,053 × 100; A1 +51.7% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: A fieldwork survey recorded the housing type of 48 households sampled in a ward of Bristol: detached 7, semi-detached 13, terraced 11, apartment 17. Test the null hypothesis that there is no preference between categories using the chi-squared test (χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E; critical value at 0.05 for 3 degrees of freedom = 7.81).
items.answer: E = 12 per category; χ² = 4.33; df = 3; not significant - accept the null hypothesis

items.stem: With reference to Delhi, India, explain how it illustrates the shifting distribution of megacities.
items.answer: The urban agglomeration reached about 32 million and is projected to become the world's largest by around 2028. The world's largest cities are moving from high-income countries to Asia.

items.stem:

items.stem:
Refer to the data below.

Population pyramids described: Village A in rural Sichuan has narrow bars for ages 20-44 and wide bars for 0-14 and 60+; District B in Shenzhen has very wide bars for ages 20-34, especially males, and narrow bars for 60+.

Describe the differences between the two pyramids.
items.answer: Village A has a deficit of working-age adults and many children and elderly; District B is dominated by young working adults with few elderly or children.

items.stem: Give one strength and one weakness of the claim that population density is the most useful indicator of population pressure on resources.
items.answer: Density is a useful starting point but must be combined with resource and development indicators.
items.markingKey: For: easy to calculate and compare between countries. Against: it ignores resource levels, technology and trade (Singapore vs Bangladesh). [4]: 1 mark for a valid argument for, 1 for its development; 1 mark for a valid argument against, 1 for its development; generic points without geographical context are capped at 2.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that government policy can successfully reduce core-periphery inequality.
items.answer: Policy can narrow but rarely eliminate inequality; success depends on long-term investment and the strength of agglomeration forces.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: China's Western Development Strategy and infrastructure (rail, roads) spread investment inland; the EU Cohesion Fund has supported growth in peripheral regions such as Poland. Against / limitations: decades of Cassa per il Mezzogiorno spending did not close Italy's north-south gap; market forces and agglomeration continue to favour the core. A supported conclusion might be: Policy can narrow but rarely eliminate inequality; success depends on long-term investment and the strength of agglomeration forces. items.stem: "Physical factors are more important than human factors in explaining global population distribution." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Physical factors set broad global limits, but human factors increasingly explain where people cluster within habitable areas.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: large empty areas coincide with deserts, ice caps and high mountains; early agricultural civilisations clustered in fertile river valleys (Nile, Indus, Huang He). Arguments challenging it: economic opportunity and technology now override physical limits (Gulf cities, Singapore); political and historical factors (colonial ports, planned capitals, migration policies) shape distribution. Evaluation should weigh places, scales, perspectives and time. Judgement: Physical factors set broad global limits, but human factors increasingly explain where people cluster within habitable areas. Paper 2 Section C markbands [15]: 13-15 thorough response to all demands including the command term; accurate, detailed geographical knowledge and terminology; well-chosen, located and quantified examples at more than one scale; explicit, balanced evaluation (perspectives, places, scales, time) with a well-substantiated conclusion. 10-12 most demands addressed; accurate knowledge; examples relevant and developed; evaluation is balanced but not sustained. 7-9 some demands addressed; knowledge mostly accurate; examples partly developed; evaluation partial or one-sided. 4-6 limited, mainly descriptive; generalised examples; little evaluation. 1-3 little relevant knowledge; no examples or evaluation. 0 does not reach the standard of the descriptors.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "backwash effect"?
options: An area with few people per km², often limited by extreme climate, relief, poor soils or remoteness
A negative feature of the place of origin that encourages people to leave, e.g. drought, landlessness, lack of services
The flow of people, capital and resources from the periphery to the core that increases regional inequality
The number of people per unit of arable (cultivable) land, a better indicator of pressure on farmland than crude density
items.answer: The flow of people, capital and resources from the periphery to the core that increases regional inequality
items.markingKey: C. "backwash effect" is the flow of people, capital and resources from the periphery to the core that increases regional inequality.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "ecumene"?
options: The diffusion of growth from the core to the periphery, e.g. through demand for raw materials and the relocation of industry
The permanently inhabited part of the Earth's surface
The movement of people within a country's borders, involving a change of permanent residence
A perceived attraction of a destination that encourages people to move there, e.g. jobs, higher wages, education
items.answer: The permanently inhabited part of the Earth's surface
items.markingKey: B. "ecumene" is the permanently inhabited part of the Earth's surface.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A perceived attraction of a destination that encourages people to move there, e.g. jobs, higher wages, education"?
items.answer: pull factor
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of pull factor.

items.stem: Explain how population change in the periphery can differ from that in the core region.
items.answer: The periphery loses young adults through out-migration, leaving an ageing population and lower birth totals; the core gains young migrants, raising natural increase and population growth.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The periphery loses young adults through out-migration, leaving an ageing population and lower birth totals; the core gains young migrants, raising natural increase and population growth. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between population distribution and population density.
items.answer: Density is a numerical measure (people per km²) for an area; distribution describes the spatial pattern of where people are located (clustered, linear, dispersed) and is shown on a dot map.
items.markingKey: Density is a numerical measure (people per km²) for an area; distribution describes the spatial pattern of where people are located (clustered, linear, dispersed) and is shown on a dot map. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Internal migration only affects the destination cities." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Source areas are also changed: loss of labour, ageing, remittance flows and the return of skills and ideas.
items.markingKey: Source areas are also changed: loss of labour, ageing, remittance flows and the return of skills and ideas. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between spread effects and backwash effects.
items.answer: Backwash effects move resources and people towards the core and increase inequality; spread effects transmit growth outward to the periphery and reduce it.
items.markingKey: Backwash effects move resources and people towards the core and increase inequality; spread effects transmit growth outward to the periphery and reduce it. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Countries with high population densities are always poor and overpopulated." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Density does not determine wealth: Singapore and the Netherlands are densely populated and rich; overpopulation depends on resources and technology relative to population.
items.markingKey: Density does not determine wealth: Singapore and the Netherlands are densely populated and rich; overpopulation depends on resources and technology relative to population. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how out-migration can affect the population structure of rural source areas.
items.answer: Loss of young adults narrows the 20-39 bars of the pyramid, leaving older people and children; birth rates fall and dependency ratios rise, e.g. "left-behind" villages in Sichuan or rural Bulgaria.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Loss of young adults narrows the 20-39 bars of the pyramid, leaving older people and children; birth rates fall and dependency ratios rise, e.g. "left-behind" villages in Sichuan or rural Bulgaria. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.markingKey: M1 urban ÷ total × 100; A1 55.2%.

items.stem: Nigeria has a population of about 223.8 million and an area of 923,768 km²; Iceland has about 0.39 million people in 103,000 km². (a) Calculate the population density of each. (b) How many times more densely populated is the denser country? (c) Explain why national density can hide uneven distribution, using one of these countries.
items.answer: (a) Nigeria: 242.3 /km²; Iceland: 3.8 /km² (b) ≈ 64.0 times (c) e.g. most people cluster in favourable areas (coasts, river valleys, cities) while deserts/mountains are almost empty.
items.markingKey: (a) A1 242.3, A1 3.8. (b) A1 64.0. (c) R1 uneven distribution explained with a physical or human factor.

items.stem: A fieldwork survey recorded reasons for moving given by 40 migrants interviewed in Shenzhen: employment 6, family 17, education 6, housing 11. Test the null hypothesis that there is no preference between categories using the chi-squared test (χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E; critical value at 0.05 for 3 degrees of freedom = 7.81).
items.answer: E = 10 per category; χ² = 8.20; df = 3; significant - reject the null hypothesis
items.markingKey: M1 expected 40/4 = 10; M1 Σ(O − E)²/E; A1 χ² = 8.20; A1 df = 3; R1 compare with 7.81: reject H₀.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Dhaka, Bangladesh shows environmental push factors in internal migration.
items.answer: The city receives an estimated 1,700 or more migrants a day, many displaced by river-bank erosion and cyclones. Environmental hazards in rural deltas add to economic push factors and accelerate urban growth.
